5.6.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * We must not withdraw from our struggle of vigilance because of dangerous despair, for [now the kingdom of God suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force] (Mt 12:11). No virtue can be attained without struggle, and the mind cannot be restrained without deep sorrow of heart, for "man is born unto trouble." And in order to reach "unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ" (Eph 13:4), we must be always in great struggle with endless care.

5.6.5.en: Fr. Serenus * Let us have great caution and diligence regarding external circumstances when we are struck by the weight of sorrow, so that we may attain the hope of receiving the things above. The mind stands to receive the heavenly things through these outward disciplines.

5.6.6.en: * [Man is born unto trouble, as the bird for flying]... Since man enjoys reason, he perceives that it is impossible for him to pass the time of his pilgrimage without sorrow. Therefore when Paul enumerated his afflictions to his disciples, he rightly added: "For yourselves know that we are appointed thereunto" (1 Thess 3:3).

5.6.7.en: For when the body is struck with blows, the mind rises up, seeking the things above. Paul again bears witness to this, saying: "Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 16:4). Thus, [man is born unto trouble, as the bird for flying], for the mind flies freely toward the heights for the very reason that the body suffers from bending downward in heaviness.

5.6.8.en: The word "man" here represents life according to the flesh. So Paul says: "For whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal" (1 Cor 3:3), and then he continues: [are ye not men?] (1 Cor 4:3) [Vulgate].

5.6.9.en: In this life [man is born unto trouble], for every carnal man, seeking temporal things, burdens his soul with the weight of his lusts.

5.6.10.en: It is a hard trouble to seek the glory of the present life, to acquire what one seeks, and to preserve it diligently when one prevails. It is a hard trouble, with endless pains, to hold on to things that you know will not last for a long time. But the saints, since they are not passionately attached to temporal things, not only do not fall under the weight of temporary lusts, but are free from weariness even when crosses arise, in these circumstances and in weaknesses.

5.6.11.en: For what is harsher than scourging? Yet it is written of the apostles when they were scourged: "And they departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name" (Acts 41:5). What can disturb the minds of those who, when they were disciplined with blows, were not troubled?

5.6.12.en: [Man is born unto trouble], because he truly feels the evils of the present state when he longs for good things... Therefore it was well added: [and the bird for flying].

5.6.13.en: The soul withdraws from the pains of trouble as it rises through hope in the things above. Was not Paul like a bird born to fly, he who endured countless crosses, saying: [Our conversation is in heaven](c)? And also: "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens" (2 Cor 1:5). He is like a bird that ascended above the lower scenes. Although he walked on the earth in the body, the two wings of hope carried him in the heavenly places.

5.6.15.en: * The fears of the struggler become for him a cause of life for his salvation, and on the contrary become shame for his enemies and mockery of them. He repels all their attacks and makes them vain, and resists all their enticements... The enemy offers Job a battle against (Satan) in the air, who moves in a terrible manner between heaven and earth. For he (Lucifer) fell from the heavens (Isa 12:14), and the saints who are on the earth did not let him rest upon it, although he desires to enjoy our destruction. For though Job defeated him many times, he did not stop the battle, not waiting for the decisive victory, but repeatedly seeks to wear out the righteous man.

5.7.s.en: 4. God is the refuge of the afflicted

5.7.0.en: 8 But I would seek unto God, and unto God would I commit my cause: 9 Which doeth great things and unsearchable; marvellous things without number: 10 Who giveth rain upon the earth, and sendeth waters upon the fields: 11 To set up on high those that be low; that those which mourn may be exalted to safety. 12 He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise. 13 He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong. 14 They meet with darkness in the daytime, and grope in the noonday as in the night. 15 But he saveth the poor from the sword, from their mouth, and from the hand of the mighty. 16 So the poor hath hope, and iniquity stoppeth her mouth. 17 Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth: therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty: 18 For he maketh sore, and bindeth up: he woundeth, and his hands make whole. 19 He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee. 20 In famine he shall redeem thee from death: and in war from the power of the sword. 21 Thou shalt be hid from the scourge of the tongue: neither shalt thou be afraid of destruction when it cometh. 22 At destruction and famine thou shalt laugh: neither shalt thou be afraid of the beasts of the earth. 23 For thou shalt be in league with the stones of the field: and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with thee. 24 And thou shalt know that thy tabernacle shall be in peace; and thou shalt visit thy habitation, and shalt lose nothing. 25 Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be great, and thine offspring as the grass of the earth. 26 Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age, like as a shock of corn cometh in in his season. 27 Lo this, we have searched it, so it is; hear it, and know thou it for thyself.

5.7.1.en: But I would seek unto God, and unto God would I commit my cause [8].

5.7.2.en: Setting aside Eliphaz's intention and his mistaken view of Job, his words are without blemish. If man, because of his transgression of God's commandment, has become born unto trouble, there is no other remedy except returning to God and relying on Him, for He is the true support of the suffering. It is as though Eliphaz says to him: If I were in your place, Job, I would not murmur and curse the day of my birth, but would take refuge in God and submit to His will, as the source of all good and consolation. I would lay my case before God; what seems good in His eyes, He will do (1 Sam 3:18). As the psalmist says: "Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass" (Ps 5:37). "I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust" (Ps 2:91). And the Apostle says: "Is any among you afflicted? let him pray" (Jas 13:5).

5.7.3.en: * Finding my state to be thus, he says, my confidence is not like yours; rather I wait, knowing that God is the Lord. You trouble yourself, but I wait for God without ceasing to call upon Him and without losing hope. For He is always able to exchange and change circumstances. I find myself in the midst of evils, but God is also able to place me in the midst of good things, transferring me from my former state to this state. He says: [The Lord is the Almighty](d), meaning that He is Lord of all, the Controller of all circumstances, and of all places and things.

5.7.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * He says to him: You are in fact not worthy to pray. I myself will call upon the Lord of all. For since you are self-assured, you no longer call upon the Lord of all, and for this reason these present evils have attacked you.

5.7.5.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * O Lord, You crown us with the shield of Your good will. What does this mean? You guard us, and make us victorious, and after the victory You give us a crown.

5.7.6.en: St. Jerome * Point out to Him what pains you, point out to Him what you desire!

5.7.7.en: * [Thou sayest to the Lord, My refuge and my fortress; my God, in him will I trust] (Ps 2:91).

5.7.8.en: Who is it that says this to the Lord? He "that dwelleth in the shelter of the most High," and not in his own shelter. Who is this who dwells in the shelter of the Most High? The one who is not proud like those two who ate (from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil) to become gods, and so lost their immortality in which they were created. They chose to dwell in their own shelter, not in the shelter of the Most High. Thus they listened to the counsel of the serpent (Gen 5:3), and disregarded God's commandment, and finally discovered that what God had threatened was fulfilled in them, and not the promise of Satan to them. Therefore let you also say: "In him I trust, he will deliver me, and I do not deliver myself.

5.7.9.en: * No one is helped by God unless he himself does something. He will be helped if he prays.

5.7.10.en: * The whole effect of faith is this: it makes us ask and receive, seek and find, knock and it is opened to us. Whereas the man who argues shuts the door of God's mercy before himself.

5.7.11.en: * You made us for Yourself, O Lord, and our hearts will not rest until they rest in You.

5.8.0.en: St. Augustine Which doeth great things and unsearchable; marvellous things without number [9].

5.8.1.en: We do not fear to entrust ourselves, as well as all our affairs, into the hands of God, for He is the Doer of great and marvelous things without limit. He is Almighty; His great works cannot be comprehended. "So that a man cannot find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end" (Eccl 3:11).

5.8.2.en: * The heretics dared to blaspheme Him... they dared to blaspheme the One whom the prophets proclaimed to be God Almighty. But as for you, worship the one God Almighty, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Flee from the error of believing in many gods. Flee from every heresy, and say: "I seek of the Almighty Lord, who doeth great things and unsearchable, and marvellous things without number"... To whom be glory forever and ever, Amen.

5.8.3.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem God is called the Worker of wonders, not as a display of His power by doing what exceeds the nature He created, nor from a desire to break its laws, since He is its Maker, but out of His love for man He works wonders, to make of His people a wonder! His surpassing love for the sons of men is exceedingly wonderful! The men of God find their delight and happiness in praising God that He is a worker of wonders!

5.8.4.en: "For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone" (Ps 86:10).

5.8.5.en: "And the heavens shall praise thy wonders, O LORD: thy faithfulness also in the congregation of the saints" (Ps 89:5).

5.8.6.en: "Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people" (Ps 96:3).

5.8.7.en: "Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him: talk ye of all his wondrous works" (Ps 105:2).

5.8.8.en: "Oh that men would praise the LORD for his goodness, and for his wonderful works to the children of men! (Ps 107:8).

5.8.9.en: "Who is he? and we will call him blessed: for wonderful things hath he done among his people" (Sir 31:9)

5.8.10.en: * He tells of the wonders of God (Ps 1:9) who sees them accomplished not only openly in the body, but also in an invisible manner in his soul; indeed these wonders are more exalted and lofty. For men, being earthly and led by what they see with the eye, marvel more that dead Lazarus rises in the body than that the persecutor Paul rises in the spirit (Jn 11; Acts 9). But the visible wonder calls the soul to enjoy the light, while through the invisible a man passes over to perceive the invisible, and so speaks of all the wonders of God.

5.8.11.en: * To rejoice in the (wonderful) works of God is to forget even yourself, since you can delight in Him alone. For what is better than He? Do you not see that when you return to yourself, you return to something sinful? "I will remember thy wonders of old" (Ps 11:77)... "Thou art the God that doest wonders" (Ps 14:77), You alone. In truth You are the great God, You work wonders in the body as in the soul, You alone are their Worker. The deaf hear, the blind see, the weak are healed, the dead rise, the paralyzed are strengthened. But these wonders were accomplished at that time in the body. Let us look at those accomplished in the soul. Those who a little while ago were drunkards have become workers, those who a little while ago were idolaters have now become believers, those who formerly robbed others have now come to give gifts to the poor.

5.8.12.en: * "The heavens shall praise thy wonders, O LORD" (Ps 5:89)... For in every work of mercy toward lost souls, every work of justification of sinners, what do we praise but the wonderful works of God? You praise Him because the dead rise; praise Him all the more because the lost have been saved. Yesterday, O man, you saw a whirlpool of drunkenness; now you see the beauty of self-control. Yesterday you saw a blasphemer of God; now you see him praising Him. Yesterday he was a slave of the creature; today he has become a worshipper of the Creator. Thus men have turned from these terrible conditions. Would that they did not look to their own merits. Let them become heavens and praise the wonders of Him who made them heavens".

5.9.0.en: St. Augustine Who giveth rain upon the earth, and sendeth waters upon the fields [10].

5.9.1.en: He gives us an example from nature of the great works of God. "Who giveth rain upon the earth." We often take rain lightly, yet it is a great work that reveals God's power; without it life could be destroyed.

5.9.2.en: In the midst of our pains and afflictions, when we cry to God, the Creator of heaven and earth, He looks upon us and covers our souls with clouds, as being His heavens, and rains upon our lives with the waters of His Holy Spirit, the Giver of heavenly consolations. So we say: "In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul" (Ps 19:94). St. Jerome sees that the clouds that cover the heavenly soul are the company of the prophets and apostles, and that the rain God gives us is His joyful commandment or His divine teachings.

5.9.3.en: * Everyone who is unworthy to understand the divine teaching, for him this teaching is covered with clouds. "Who prepareth rain for the earth" (Ps 8:147). The earth needs rain; if our earth does not receive the rain, which is the fountain of divine teaching, it brings forth no fruit.

5.9.4.en: * Moses was a cloud, therefore he says: "My doctrine shall drop as the rain" (Deut 32:2). His message is a spiritual rain that comes down upon us. In real fact, what does Paul say in his epistle to the Hebrews? "For the earth which drinketh in the rain that cometh oft upon it" (Heb 7:6). Again he says: [I have planted, Apollos watered] (Col 6:3).

5.9.5.en: * The clouds are the prophets and apostles who water the barren hearts of men with the rains of their teachings.

5.9.6.en: St. Jerome Pope Gregory (the Great) translates this verse, "Who sendeth waters upon the fields," as "upon all things," and says that man represents all things. For the greatest of wonders is the creation of man, who represents the whole universe: [Man shares existence with stones, life with trees, sensation with animals, and discernment with angels. He truly represents the title "the universe," for in him the whole universe is contained. Thus the Truth says to His disciples: "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature" (cf. Mt 19:28-20). For all creation is for man alone, in whom was created what is common to all things.]

5.9.7.en: * The human man had not yet entered the world of beings (that is, until the sixth day)... For it is not fitting for the ruler to appear before the appearance of the things over which he rules.

5.9.8.en: But as soon as his dominion was ready, the Creator having prepared all things as a royal dwelling for the coming king, the ruler was announced!

5.9.9.en: This royal dwelling is the earth, the islands, the sea, and the heaven, which is like an arch encircling above all, like a roof to it.

5.9.10.en: In this palace He stored up wealth of every kind: the whole world of plants and animals, everything that has body, breath, and life. And if anyone wished to count material things as wealth, he would find also all that is beautiful and valuable in man's eyes, of gold, silver, and precious stones, to enjoy.

5.9.11.en: The Creator hid these things in abundance in the bosom of the earth, as if they were a royal treasure, so that when the human man appeared in the world, he might contemplate some of them and rule over the others. For when he enjoys these things he thanks the Giver of good things. And when he beholds the beauty of the things he sees and their vastness, he is drawn to the great, incomprehensible power of their Creator.

5.9.12.en: St. Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa * The Almighty gives rain upon the earth when He waters the dry hearts of the Gentiles with the grace of the heavenly preaching, and sends waters upon all things, since by the fullness of the Spirit He turns the barrenness of lost man to fruitfulness, as the Truth Himself says with His lips: [Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst] (Jn 14:4).

5.10.0.en: To set up on high those that be low; that those which mourn may be exalted to safety [11].

5.10.1.en: The next example is God's power that is manifested in the humble, whom the Most High lifts up, and His work in the life of the mourners, giving them safety.

5.10.2.en: The successive calamities drove Job down to the dunghill, as he no longer had a place to dwell and rest. But since he humbles himself without murmuring, he comes to be on high, that is, he soars in the heavens, for humility is the ladder by which the soul ascends in Christ Jesus to the bosom of the Father.

5.10.3.en: Truly sorrow crushes man so that he becomes like one descending into bitterness and destruction, but when he mourns in the Lord he ascends to true safety.

5.11.0.en: He disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise [12].

5.11.1.en: The third example is God's intervention in the affairs of men; for although He has granted them freedom of will, He does not leave matters to go on without control, for He [disappointeth the devices of the crafty], so their hands are not left to settle upon the heads of the righteous.

5.11.2.en: By taking refuge in God the believer enjoys the divine truth, so the crafty cannot lay their hands on the believer. Falsehood and deceit cannot appear in the presence of the truth, for the truth is a light that dispels falsehood (darkness). So in the midst of noonday their life becomes an exceedingly dark night. The kingdom of light does not reign over them; rather the kingdom of darkness dominates them.

5.11.3.en: Often the Jewish leaders, in their craftiness, thought they could trap the Lord Christ, but He allowed them to test Him, and through their craftiness they judged themselves by themselves. For craftiness and deceit cannot stand before judgment, but carry corruption within themselves.

5.11.4.en: * When they scheme with evil things they show themselves for what they are, and since they cannot accomplish their purposes, (God) preserves those against whom they plot evils.

5.12.0.en: He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong [13].

5.12.1.en: The Apostle Paul quoted this verse in his First Epistle to the Corinthians (1 Cor 3:19).

5.12.2.en: God can with surpassing ease demolish the plots of the crafty, who reckon in themselves that they are wise, so that none is able to stand before them. He has brought to nothing, and brings to nothing, the counsels of many, such as the counsel of Ahithophel, who planned for Absalom to kill his father David and take his throne, and He also brought to nothing the counsel of Sanballat (Neh 4:7-23), and the counsel of Haman (Esth 8). Truly every instrument formed against the Church of God shall not prosper (Isa 54:17).

5.12.3.en: "In the net which they hid is their own foot taken" (Ps 9:15). "He is fallen into the ditch which he made. His mischief shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down upon his own pate" (Ps 7:15-16).

5.12.4.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) gives us two examples of how God takes the wise in their craftiness, the first from the Old Testament and the second from the New. In the Old Testament Joseph's brothers wanted to be rid of their brother lest he rise above them and they be subject to his authority, and according to their human wisdom they sold him as a slave. God used this action of theirs, and by His divine providence he became great in Egypt, and they bowed down before him. The second is the wisdom of the Hebrews in the New Testament, where the priests and religious leaders wanted to be rid of Him lest the whole world go after the Lord Christ (Jn 19:21); they sentenced Him to death, and behold, by that very means - the Cross - the whole world went after Him.

5.12.5.en: * How does God take the wise in their craftiness? In that, while they think they are able to work without God, they find themselves all the more in need of Him. They fall into a predicament to show that they are less than fishermen and the unlearned, who now cannot work without their wisdom.

5.12.6.en: St. John Chrysostom * The ruler flattered Jesus (Lk 18:18), and tried to deceive Him, pretending to take a sympathetic position toward Him. But what did He who knows all things answer, as it is written of Him: [He taketh the wise in their own craftiness] (Job 13:5)?

5.13.0.en: St. Cyril the Great They meet with darkness in the daytime, and grope in the noonday as in the night [14].

5.13.1.en: The true believer's life is a continuous day without darkness, and as the Apostle says: "Ye are all the children of light, and the children of the day: we are not of the night, nor of darkness" (1 Thess 5:5). Lot did not know darkness when he received the two angels and urged them to be his guests and spend the night in his house, but the wicked were in darkness and did not realize that they were two angels of light, so they wanted to know them and commit corrupting evil with them, and the men were struck with blindness, and became like those in darkness and were unable to find the door of the house (Gen 11:19). Thus, instead of enjoying the angelic light they fell into the darkness of evil, and lost their inner and outer sight.

5.13.2.en: * "They meet with darkness in the daytime," because in the presence of the Truth Himself they were struck blind by the deceit of unbelief... Thus the Light Himself counsels them, saying: "Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you" (Jn 35:12).

5.13.3.en: When the wicked see their neighbors doing something good, they are stricken with the pain of their envy, and suffer the torments of their painful malice, when they see with their envy-filled hearts good things in others. Therefore it was well said: "They meet with darkness in the daytime," when their minds are grieved at the loftiness of another, a shadow is cast from the ray of light...

5.13.4.en: They busy themselves with zeal and intense examination to find something with which they can accuse others. They truly see all the members sound, but with the eyes of their closed hearts they seek to find in the emotions an affliction for others...

5.13.6.en: * The worst thing about envy is that it is a disease folded away in secrecy. You see the envious man with lowered eyes and a gloomy face, constantly complaining of an inner torment which withers his face and wastes his body, so that he grows lean and weak. He is ashamed to say: "I am envious, I feel bitterness and grief at the good that another man has obtained, and I am tormented by the happiness of my friends, and cannot bear the success of my peers. I see that the happiness of others is a sword that tears my bowels and stabs me to the heart." This is what the envious man ought to have confessed. But he prefers to keep it in his heart and be silent, and so the disease remains in him, and the torment wastes him, and his body perishes little by little.

5.13.7.en: St. Basil the Great * Beasts, birds and creeping things grieve at the sufferings of their kinds in nature, and cooperate together against those who oppose them, but the envious man does the opposite; he rejoices at the fall of the brother and the neighbor and the stranger and the relative and the friend.

5.13.8.en: * The envious man counts the misfortunes of others a benefit to himself more than any success of his own... becoming like a common enemy against mankind and a slap to the members of the Church. For what is nearer to madness than envy?!

5.13.9.en: * Satan is envious, but he envies mankind, and does not envy another satan, whereas you are a man who envies your brother man, especially those of your own family and clan, which Satan does not do.

5.13.10.en: * There is no disease worse than envy and malice, for on its basis death entered the world (Wis 2:24), because when the devil saw man honored he could not bear his well-being, and did all he could until he killed him. By envy Abel was slain, and David was nearly killed, and many others of the righteous were killed, and the Jews became the killers of Christ.

5.14.0.en: St. John Chrysostom But he saveth the poor from the sword, from their mouth, and from the hand of the mighty [15].

5.14.1.en: The counsel of the crafty aims at destroying the poor, but God delivers them from their sword as well as from their mouth and their hands. He is the Controller of all, He works on behalf of the poor, and neither the counsels of the wicked nor their strong hands nor their swords stand before Him.

5.14.2.en: When the believer casts his whole life into the hand of the Lord, he does not fear the devil's sword that kills the soul, nor does he lose his hope because of this mighty one. For although the devil carries the sword of slander and destruction, and is a murderer from the beginning, yet He who is with us is greater than he who is against us. With us is our God, who delivers by Himself, and who also sends His angels to guard us. In Him you enjoy hope, and despair cannot dominate our hearts or our thoughts.

5.14.3.en: * "The voice of the LORD breaketh the cedars" (Ps 29:5), for Christ is baptized, and the demons that were formerly swollen and haughty are shattered in a heap of ruin [The Lord breaks them. Like a calf, He hurls them into the air like pieces of trees and scatters them to far places in pieces].

5.14.4.en: * "Hold thy peace" (Mk 25:1)! Let your silence be praise to me. I do not ask for your voice to praise me, but your torment and punishment are praise to me. I am not pleased by your praise of me; I rejoice in your departure. [Hold thy peace, and come out of the man] (cf. Mk 25:1). As if He says: Come out of my dwelling; what are you doing in my guest chamber? I want to enter. Hold your peace and come out of the man (the rational animal). Come out of the man, leave the guest chamber that was prepared for me. The Lord wants His dwelling... It is not my will that you possess him... I have taken a human body... The body that you now possess shares in my body; come out of it!

5.14.5.en: * They aim to shoot their arrows in the darkness at the upright heart... for I stand in the line of battle, vigilant and girded, ready for the fight. I will not neglect the struggle that has begun, especially since you say that they have bent the strings of their bows, and the arrows are made ready in their quiver, and behold, they wait in the darkness to wound my saints, but they are not yet able to aim them. They have drawn the string, they have filled the quiver. They are ready to aim their arrows in the darkness at the sincere heart. Now that they are fully prepared I place myself among them, and stand opposite their arrows, so that even by my pain my servants may not feel pain, and by my wounds they are healed, and by my sufferings they do not suffer, but say: "Thou compassest him with favour as with a shield" (Ps 5:12).

5.14.6.en: St. Jerome * He adds that God does the opposite when He shows concern for the weak. [He gives the weak hope, and stops the mouths of the unjust](f)... Eliphaz was busy establishing a dialogue by which he belittles Job. But it is God's custom to lift up the weak, abase the strong and put the deceivers to shame.

5.15.0.en: St. John Chrysostom So the poor hath hope, and iniquity stoppeth her mouth [16].

5.15.1.en: When the afflicted looks at the crafty he collapses in despair, but when he looks to God he is filled with hope, so the mouths of the crafty are stopped, and the sin lying hidden in them cannot utter a word, for God Himself has spoken.

5.15.2.en: * Even if these (evil) powers rise and prevail, know that this is God's discipline, for although they triumph, they will be judged with a just judgment. Be sure of this, that the beast will be slaughtered at the appointed time. But you, my brother, be zealous in seeking mercy so that there may be peace for the people of God.

5.16.0.en: St. Aphrahat Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth: therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty [17].

5.16.1.en: Eliphaz distinguishes between the Lord's discipline of His believers and the punishment He imposes on the wicked. He esteems God's fatherly discipline of the believer when he falls.

5.16.2.en: At the end of his first speech Eliphaz offers a consolation which Eliphaz himself needed, namely, accepting the discipline of the Lord Almighty.

5.16.3.en: What befell Job was nothing but discipline from the loving Almighty God. And it is folly and madness to quarrel with the Lord and ignore His tender fatherhood even in the very moments of discipline.

5.16.4.en: The Hebrew word translated "despise not" means "do not hate," so it is fitting for the believer to submit gladly to God's will and disciplines, even if they are bitter, for we need the rod of discipline, and let us reckon that what befalls us we deserve, and it is a bitter medicine useful for our healing.

5.16.5.en: It also means: do not think ill of Him, and do not belittle what He has done, but bow before Him and trust in His wisdom and providence.

5.16.6.en: It also means: do not overlook Him, as though what has befallen were by chance, and not from a wise and well-ordered divine plan. Reckon discipline to be the voice of the Lord and His heavenly message.

5.16.7.en: Thus it is fitting for us to accept the Lord's discipline, and appreciate His wisdom, and submit to Him with fear and trembling, confident that it is for our eternal edification. He weans us from the world and temporal goods so that we may cling to the Giver of goods Himself, and He prepares us for eternal glory.

5.16.8.en: How beautiful it is for a leader to direct himself and those around him to the blessings of the Lord's discipline of His believers. For though it has bitterness and troubles, it is not destructive; it is temporary, and gives strength for the believer to stand even before the beasts of the earth, because he feels that what befalls him is by God's permission for his edification, correction and approval.

5.16.9.en: But Eliphaz's aim here is not to encourage Job to accept suffering from the hand of God, but he is claiming that God does not seek his discipline but his destruction, because he has transgressed the limits, and thus his sufferings are nothing but punishment, and though they seem exceedingly severe, they are only a pledge of what Job should expect on the day of judgment, because he is the worst of the wicked.

5.16.10.en: * The pomegranate is covered with a hard and bitter rind; this outer rind is not fit to eat, but the inside is beautiful to look at, and has carefully arranged seeds, and tastes sweet. So also is the life of philosophy (spiritual wisdom): it appears dry and unpleasant from the outside, but when it ripens it is full of good hopes. And when the gardener (God) opens the pomegranate of life at the proper time and reveals its hidden beauty, those who taste it enjoy its sweetness. And the Apostle Paul says: "Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous (that is, the first impression of the pomegranate with regard to its rind): nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby" (Heb 12:11) (that is, the sweetness of the fruit within).

5.17.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa For he maketh sore, and bindeth up: he woundeth, and his hands make whole [18].

5.17.1.en: Although God allowed the sores in Job's body as bitter wounds, He is a skilled surgeon who binds up the inner wounds of the soul, and grants it the healing consolations of His Holy Spirit.

5.17.2.en: In His discipline He seems to crush, but He restores to His believers every honor and glory on an eternal level; thus His hands make whole. Moses the prophet sings: "Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil" (Ps 90:15). And Hosea the prophet says: "He hath torn, and he will heal us" (Hos 6:1).

5.17.3.en: * In wounding, He heals. For when we are pierced by the spear of His fear, He restores us to a sound mind.

5.17.5.en: * Therefore if anyone at any time sees evil in many persons, yet God's wrath does not fall on all, but only on some, he must realize that discipline is applied with love to the human race. For the blows do not fall on everyone, but the blows that fall on some discipline all, that they may turn back from evil.

5.17.6.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * "For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth" (Heb 12:6). First He wounds, and afterward He heals. He brings pain and then binds up.

5.17.7.en: In the same vein He says: "See, I have this day set thee over the nations and over the kingdoms, to root out, and to pull down, and to destroy, and to throw down, to build, and to plant" (Jer 1:10). However it may be, it is first necessary to remove what is bad from us (from within us), for God cannot build where there is a mean building. For what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? (2 Cor 6:14).

5.17.8.en: Evil must be uprooted from its roots, the building of evil must be pulled down from our souls, so that the Word may build and plant.

5.17.9.en: * When evils are not first removed, we do not receive goodness. He breaks down the feeble buildings of unbelief, for He is the Lord who builds the true tabernacle, which He makes and not man (Heb 8:2), of which Paul said: "Ye are... God's building" (1 Cor 3:9).

5.17.10.en: * "Nevertheless in those days, saith the LORD, I will not make a full end with you" (Jer 5:18)...

5.17.11.en: God delays His condemnation of those who deserve punishment, to give them a chance to repent. He does not punish sin at once, and does not inflict destruction on the sinner, but delays the punishment.

5.17.12.en: We find an example of this in the Book of Leviticus: in the curses spoken to those who transgress the Law, after announcing the first punishments, it is said: "And if ye will not yet for all this hearken unto me, then I will punish you seven times more for your sins" (Lev 26:18). Then it also mentions another punishment: "And if ye will not for all this hearken unto me, but walk contrary unto me; Then I will walk contrary unto you also in fury" (Lev 26:27-28). From this it is clear to us that God inflicts punishments very slowly, because He wants to lead the sinner to repentance rather than make him pay the price immediately.

5.17.13.en: This is also what happened with the people; the Lord threatened them with the sufferings that would befall them, and then said to them afterward: "Nevertheless in those days... I will not make a full end with you."

5.17.14.en: * "For this is the time of the LORD'S vengeance." Holy Scripture shows that punishments are inflicted on the man who bears them and is patient in bearing them. When a man is not punished on earth he remains so, without punishment, because he is to be punished on the day of judgment. And the Lord says by the mouth of Hosea the prophet: "I will not punish your daughters when they commit whoredom, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery" (Hos 4:14). God does not punish sinners because of His anger against them, as some think, or in other words, when God inflicts punishment on a sinful man, He does not inflict it out of anger at this man, but on the contrary, the sign of God's anger against a man consists in not inflicting punishment on him. For the punished man, even if he suffers under the effect of this punishment, yet the aim is his correction and reformation. As David says: [O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure] (Ps 6:1). If you wish to discipline me, as Jeremiah says: "O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing" (Jer 10:24). Many have been reformed by the Lord's punishments and disciplines of them. As the Scripture says, when the sons of the Lord Christ sin they are punished so that they may have a chance for mercy from the Lord: "If his children forsake my law, and walk not in my judgments; If they break my statutes, and keep not my commandments; Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes. Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him" (Ps 89:30-33).

5.17.15.en: From this we understand that if someone commits sins and has not been punished until now, it is a sign that he does not yet deserve punishment.

5.18.0.en: Origen He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee [19].

5.18.1.en: The previous speech was general, but now he addresses Job directly, offering him God's precious promises and announcing His great mercies.

5.18.2.en: Truly Job's friends were not guided by the Spirit of God in all that they said, but they offered divine promises they knew through oral tradition. Though at times they spoke things that were not right about God and about Job.

5.18.3.en: By saying: "He shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee," he affirms the repetition of afflictions and troubles, along with the repetition of help and deliverance. As long as we are in the world we expect afflictions, but we trust in the help of God our Father and His concern for our salvation and peace. The Apostle Paul says: "What persecutions I endured: but out of them all the Lord delivered me" (2 Tim 3:11).

5.18.4.en: "No evil touch thee": afflictions will not cause real harm, for the wicked one does not touch God's children (1 Jn 5:18), but they are kept in the hand of God their Savior.

5.18.5.en: * What does the number six, followed by the number seven, indicate but weariness in the period of the present life? For God, after completing everything on the sixth day, created man and rested on the seventh day. This very seventh day has no evening, since there is no end afterward to end the rest that followed. When all things were completed, rest followed; so after the good works of the present life comes the reward of eternal rest. Therefore "in six troubles" the Lord delivers you, and so "in seven there shall no evil touch thee." For by the direction of fatherly tenderness He trains us in the troubles of the present life. But at the coming of the Judge He hides us from calamity... but brings us to His more assured salvation.

5.18.7.en: * If Job is one of those whom God warns and reforms, and not of those whom He strikes with punishment and destruction, then in six troubles God delivers him, these that wear him out, but since he is His servant and friend and soldier, evil will not touch him the seventh time, for God's help preserves him. But it seems that the case is not so, as Eliphaz meant. Here the calamity that befell you the first time is the burning of the flock, and the second the raid on the oxen, the third the loss of the she-asses, the fourth the plundering of the camels, the fifth the death of the herdsmen, the sixth the sudden death of your sons and daughters, and after that the seventh, evil has touched you, namely the bodily pain and the sores of your members. In any case, God does not deliver you, He who strikes and heals, who causes pain and cures, that you may deserve the divine visitation.

5.18.8.en: What Eliphaz said he meant to lead Job to despair. He did not know that this encouraged the wrestler all the more. For God delivered him six times from troubles, for the six calamities we have now enumerated came upon him from the enemy. But God, looking at the righteous man, had set beforehand limits that the enemy could not exceed. [Behold, here I deliver him to you, but respect his soul] (cf. Job 12:1). That is: [You may touch what is outside him, but these words will not give you authority to enter into him within]... Note how God preserved Job from these trials, and in vain Eliphaz said to Job the former and the latter things.

5.18.9.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Note how he destroys all benefit in what he says and delivers a violent blow. How and by what means? By showing that Job was not a party among those who receive a warning, nor among those who obtain hope. But in reality what he said applies entirely to the person of Job. But his speech had its general application, for he said that this is what we have seen and heard. So if this did not happen in your case, if you remain in your troubles, they are for your benefit, that you may know your error.

5.19.0.en: St. John Chrysostom In famine he shall redeem thee from death: and in war from the power of the sword [20].

5.19.1.en: Famine will not be able to destroy them, for "in the days of famine they shall be satisfied" (Ps 37:19). "To deliver their soul from death, and to keep them alive in famine" (Ps 33:19). Man needs the Word of God - not only as the Savior who restores man's soul to its first nature, but also to satisfy all needs. He presents Himself to man as everything to him. For in the Lord Christ famine cannot destroy us, for the Lord is our satisfaction. Christ offers Himself to those who feel they need Him. For this feeling grants them the worthiness of His presence and dwelling in their hearts. He is one, offering Himself to each believer according to his spiritual state.

5.19.2.en: * Perhaps, as the Apostle says of those [who have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil] (Heb 14:5), Christ has become each of these things, so as to suit the different senses of the soul.

5.19.3.en: For He was called the true Light, so that the eyes of the soul may find something that enlightens them.

5.19.4.en: And He is (the Logos) λόγος, so that its ears may find something to hear.

5.19.5.en: Then He is the bread of life, so that the soul may find something to taste.

5.19.6.en: And in a way He was called spikenard or ointment, so that the soul's sense of smell may perceive the fragrant aroma of the Word.

5.19.7.en: And for the same reason it was also said that He can be felt and held, and He was called the incarnate Logos, so that the inner hand of the soul may touch Him with regard to the Word of life (Jn 1:1-4; 1 Jn 1:1).

5.19.8.en: But all these things are the One - the Word of God Himself - who adapts to the various passions of the one who prays, according to those many names, and so leaves none of the faculties of the soul empty of His grace.

5.19.9.en: * Truly, I can say that He becomes everything that every creature capable of being set free needs. Therefore He becomes the light of men, if they - while in the darkness of evils - seek that light which shineth in the darkness and which the darkness comprehended not. He would not have become a light for men had they not been in darkness.
